title: Add file-like tools for forge issues and pull requests
body:
<!-- mach12-issue -->

## Summary

Scramjet lacks first-class, permission-separable tools for reading and modifying forge issues and pull requests. Agents currently rely on `bash` plus forge-specific CLI commands, which prevents read-only agents from accessing these artifacts safely and makes precise edits substantially more token-intensive than file edits.

## User's Request

- Consider `read_issue`, `write_issue`, `read_pr`, and `write_pr` as suggested names.
- Revisit those names carefully because the existing harness has three distinct file operations: `read`, `write`, and `edit`. The proposed capability spans all three semantics, so literal parity may call for a different tool split or naming scheme.
- Provide an interface as close as practical to the existing file tools so agents can read ranges, reread after external changes, and make precise edits without rewriting an entire artifact.
- Treat an issue or pull request as a deterministic plaintext document whose lines represent its body and comments.
- Require the agent to read an issue or pull request before mutating it.
- Back the tools with `gh` for GitHub repositories and `glab` for GitLab repositories, selected from the current working directory's remote.
- Keep read capabilities independently grantable from mutation capabilities and from `bash`, so read-only agents can inspect forge artifacts without gaining shell or write access.
- Return actionable failures. Missing authentication should direct the agent to help the user authenticate with the corresponding CLI; other CLI failures should expose the attempted command and failure details so an agent with `bash` can recover when appropriate.
- On Scramjet startup, warn when the CLI required by the current repository's forge is missing or unauthenticated. Do not require or warn about the unrelated forge CLI.
- Do not create a temporary on-disk mirror or working copy of an issue or pull request. The artifact representation should exist only in tool results and session history.
- Determine whether file-like write semantics can cleanly support creating new issues, pull requests, and comments as well as changing existing content.

## Investigation

- The built-in `read` tool accepts a path plus optional 1-indexed `offset` and `limit`, truncates large output, and emits continuation guidance (`packages/coding-agent/src/core/tools/read.ts:20-24`, `packages/coding-agent/src/core/tools/read.ts:280-324`).
- The built-in `write` tool accepts complete content, creates a missing file, and overwrites an existing file. Its prompt guidance reserves it for new files and complete rewrites (`packages/coding-agent/src/core/tools/write.ts:14-17`, `packages/coding-agent/src/core/tools/write.ts:181-224`).
- The built-in `edit` tool performs one or more exact, unique, non-overlapping text replacements against the original content and returns a unified diff (`packages/coding-agent/src/core/tools/edit.ts:31-63`, `packages/coding-agent/src/core/tools/edit.ts:294-384`).
- `edit` rereads the current file inside its mutation operation, but its schema does not establish that the model previously invoked `read` (`packages/coding-agent/src/core/tools/edit.ts:309-384`).
- Scramjet can register model-callable tools with independent names, schemas, prompt metadata, execution, and rendering. Tool allowlists can select extension and built-in tools by name (`packages/coding-agent/src/core/extensions/types.ts:465-525`, `packages/coding-agent/src/core/agent-session.ts:976-997`).
- Current Mach 12 issue and pull-request reads are delegate-only commands that use `bash` and `gh`, return complete bodies and comments, and do not expose offset/limit or precise-edit interfaces (`packages/scramjet/mach12/commands/mach12:gh-issue-read.md:1-7`, `packages/scramjet/mach12/commands/mach12:gh-issue-read.md:19-52`, `packages/scramjet/mach12/commands/mach12:gh-pr-read.md:19-52`).
- Closed predecessor #33 introduced delegate-only `gh-*` command primitives, explicitly deferred a future `glab-*` family and forge-selection mechanism, and did not add first-class permission-separable tools.
- Existing product forge detection checks only the `origin` remote for the literal `github.com` host and silently returns no result for GitLab, host aliases, self-hosted forges, missing CLIs, and authentication failures (`packages/scramjet/src/pr-indicator.ts:37-57`).
- Scramjet's vision document identifies `glab` equivalents and forge interchangeability as deferred work; current executable forge subroutines use `gh` (`packages/scramjet/docs/scramjet-vision.md:1023-1035`).
- Tool execution failures become model-visible error results when execution throws, providing an existing mechanism for actionable CLI diagnostics (`packages/agent/src/agent-loop.ts:627-660`).

## Analysis

The requested parity is behavioral rather than a literal copy of the current `write` schema. Full-content overwrite semantics fit artifact creation or complete replacement, while token-efficient, conflict-aware changes align with `edit`; collapsing both into a single vaguely named mutation tool could obscure permissions and increase the risk of overwriting concurrent changes.

A plaintext artifact representation must be deterministic enough for range reads and exact replacement. It also needs unambiguous boundaries and identities for metadata, bodies, top-level comments, and any supported review discussion so line changes map back to one remote object without temporary files.

Read-before-mutation enforcement requires more than rereading inside the mutation implementation: the tool family must recognize a prior successful model-visible read and define what happens when the remote artifact changes afterward. Exact replacement can detect many stale edits, but creation, whole-body replacement, deleted comments, and unrelated concurrent changes need explicit conflict behavior to avoid silent data loss.

Forge selection and startup diagnostics also need stronger repository resolution than the current GitHub-only PR indicator. Missing repositories, absent or multiple remotes, aliases, self-hosted instances, authentication for the wrong host, insufficient scopes, network failures, timeouts, malformed CLI output, and inaccessible artifacts must remain distinguishable rather than collapsing into “not found.”

## Proposed Behavior

Scramjet provides a file-like tool experience for issues and pull requests while keeping forge reads, forge mutations, and shell access independently grantable. The final names and schema split preserve the meaningful distinctions among reading, complete creation/replacement, and precise editing; the four proposed names are the starting point, not a requirement to hide those distinctions.

Reads produce a deterministic, line-addressable plaintext rendering with bounded output and continuation support. Mutations require a prior successful read of the target, apply changes to explicitly identified body or comment content, and fail visibly when the requested change cannot be reconciled with the current remote state.

The current repository determines whether `gh` or `glab` is used. Startup reports only actionable prerequisites for the detected forge, while each tool reports missing executables, authentication problems, authorization failures, and other CLI errors with enough safe detail for recovery.

No issue or pull-request representation is mirrored to disk for agent interaction. Tool calls, results, and normal session persistence are the only local representation exposed to the agent.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `(user-stated)` The design explicitly evaluates `read_issue`, `write_issue`, `read_pr`, and `write_pr` as suggested names and accounts for the existing `read`/`write`/`edit` distinction before finalizing the public tool surface.
- [ ] `(user-stated)` An agent granted forge-read tools but not forge-mutation tools or `bash` can read issues and pull requests from the current repository.
- [ ] `(user-stated)` Issue and pull-request reads support bounded range access and rereading through a deterministic plaintext representation that includes supported body and comment content.
- [ ] `(user-stated)` Mutating an existing issue or pull request is rejected unless the agent has first successfully read the relevant artifact.
- [ ] `(user-stated)` Existing artifact content can be changed precisely without requiring the model to resend the entire issue or pull-request document.
- [ ] `(derived)` A stale, ambiguous, or conflicting mutation fails visibly and does not silently discard unrelated remote changes.
- [ ] `(user-stated)` GitHub repositories use `gh`, GitLab repositories use `glab`, and the unrelated CLI is neither required nor warned about.
- [ ] `(user-stated)` Interactive startup warns when the CLI required for the detected current repository is missing or unauthenticated.
- [ ] `(user-stated)` Tool errors distinguish missing CLI, missing authentication, and other command failures; authentication errors provide recovery guidance, while other failures include the safely rendered attempted command and diagnostic output.
- [ ] `(user-stated)` The tools do not create a temporary on-disk issue or pull-request mirror or working copy.
- [ ] `(derived)` The supported semantics for creating issues, pull requests, and comments are explicitly decided, documented, and tested; unsupported creation operations fail clearly rather than being inferred from mutation behavior.
- [ ] `(derived)` Large artifacts use bounded tool output with a lossless continuation path and remain available through normal session history.
- [ ] `(derived)` Forge identifiers, artifact numbers, body/comment boundaries, and user-provided content are passed to CLI processes as data rather than interpolated into shell source.
- [ ] `(derived)` Automated tests cover permission separation, read-before-mutation enforcement, concurrent remote changes, forge selection, startup prerequisites, CLI failures, and plaintext rendering round trips.

## Open Questions

- Should parity produce six obvious tools (`read_*`, `write_*`, and `edit_*`), retain the four suggested names with mutation modes, or use another split that keeps permissions and semantics clear?
- What locator replaces a file path, including explicit repository selection when the current working directory is ambiguous or absent?
- Which pull-request content belongs in the plaintext document: description and conversation comments only, or also reviews, inline review threads, status data, and other metadata?
- How should stable body/comment boundaries and identities appear without making normal reads unnecessarily verbose?
- What prior-read evidence and remote version information should mutation require, and how long should that evidence remain valid across turns, resumes, and external changes?
- Should write-like creation cover new issues, pull requests, top-level comments, review comments, or only a subset, and how should newly assigned identifiers and URLs be returned?
- How should GitLab merge-request terminology map to the proposed `*_pr` names?
- How should forge detection handle multiple remotes, non-`origin` remotes, SSH host aliases, GitHub Enterprise, self-managed GitLab, detached worktrees, and repositories without remotes?
- Which startup conditions warrant proactive warnings versus tool-time errors, especially offline operation, expired credentials, insufficient scopes, inaccessible repositories, and transient network failures?

## Technical Notes

- Existing file-tool schemas, truncation behavior, diff rendering, and tool prompt metadata are useful interface precedents, but a remote forge artifact should not be disguised as a local path or implemented through a temporary file.
- `pi.exec` already supports argument-array process execution, cancellation, timeouts, and captured stdout/stderr; the existing PR indicator and GitHub autocomplete example demonstrate startup-time CLI calls but do not provide the required diagnostics or forge coverage.
- The current `gh-*` Mach 12 subroutines and predecessor #33 contain pagination, completeness, and delegation patterns that may inform the tool behavior, but they are bash-authorized command prose rather than permission-separable first-class tools.
